vowel_formants.speaker: adult male, citation monosyllables
vowel_formants.source: Wu Zongji 1986 (table reproduced in Lin & Wang 1992)
vowel_formants.notes: Older spectrograph measurements from few speakers. F1 of /a/ (1000 Hz) is higher than later studies of male speakers usually report, so treat it as an upper bound. The low F3 of the retroflex apical vowel is its main cue.

contrasts: aspirated versus unaspirated in every stop and affricate (p pʰ, t tʰ, k kʰ, ts tsʰ, tʂ tʂʰ, tɕ tɕʰ); no voicing contrast in obstruents
three sibilant places: dental (ts tsʰ s), retroflex (tʂ tʂʰ ʂ, with ɻ) and alveolo-palatal (tɕ tɕʰ ɕ)
four lexical tones plus a toneless (neutral) syllable type
alveolar versus velar nasal coda (n, ŋ)
front rounded y against i and u
allophony: after ts tsʰ s the high vowel is a syllabic dental approximant [ɹ̩] (traditional ɿ), after tʂ tʂʰ ʂ ɻ a syllabic retroflex approximant [ɻ̩] (traditional ʅ); both are voiced continuations of the consonant constriction (Lee-Kim 2014)
the alveolo-palatals tɕ tɕʰ ɕ occur only before i, y and the glides j, ɥ, where dentals, retroflexes and velars never occur; they are in complementary distribution with all three series
the retroflex series is apical post-alveolar with a sublingual cavity, not fully curled back (Ladefoged & Wu 1984)
the low vowel is [a] in open syllables and before i and n, [ɑ] before u and ŋ, and [ɛ] between a palatal glide and n (ian [jɛn], üan [ɥɛn])
the mid vowel is [ɤ] in an open syllable, [e] before i and after j or ɥ, [o] before u and after w, and [ə] before n and ŋ
pinyin r is an approximant [ɻ] with weak frication at most, often transcribed [ʐ]
x varies from velar [x] to uvular [χ] or glottal [h]
coda n and ŋ are often realised as nasalisation of the vowel with incomplete oral closure
unaspirated stops and affricates may be voiced between vowels in neutral-tone syllables (bàba [pa.bə])
w is often labiodental [ʋ] before non-back vowels in Beijing speech
syllables written with an initial vowel may begin with a glottal stop or a weak velar or glottal fricative (zero initial)
high vowels may devoice after voiceless fricatives and aspirates in neutral-tone syllables (dòufu)
syllable_structure: (C)(G)V(X) plus tone, where G is j, w or ɥ and X is n, ŋ or an offglide i or u; ɚ and erhua rhymes add a rhotic coda
phonotactics: no consonant clusters; the only codas are n and ŋ (and the rhotic of erhua)
no final stops and no final m
labials combine with w only before o (bo, po, mo, fo); f does not precede i or y
apical vowels only after the dental and retroflex sibilants; alveolo-palatals only before high front vowels and glides
erhua merges the suffix -r with the rhyme: codas n and i are dropped, a velar nasal coda leaves nasalisation on the rhotacised vowel
every full syllable is heavy (long vowel, diphthong or vowel plus nasal); neutral-tone syllables are light

stress.type: no contrastive word stress; full-toned (heavy) versus neutral-tone (light) syllables
stress.rule: Every full-toned syllable is prominent and neutral-tone syllables are weak; in a word of two full syllables the last is usually slightly longer in citation (Chao 1968), though Duanmu (2007) analyses words as trochaic.
stress.cues: duration and expansion of the tonal pitch range; intensity is secondary; vowel quality reduces only in neutral-tone syllables

rhythm.vowel_reduction: moderate, only in neutral-tone syllables: vowels centralise, diphthongs simplify, codas weaken
rhythm.notes: Less strictly syllable-timed than Cantonese because of neutral-tone reduction (Mok 2009).

length.notes: No length contrast. The vowel of an open full syllable is long, vowels before a coda are short, so full rhymes have about equal weight; neutral-tone syllables are about half to 60 percent as long as full syllables (Lin & Yan 1980).

voice_onset_time_ms.source: Chao & Chen 2008; Rochet & Fei 1991 report longer aspirated values, near 100 ms, in isolated words

intonation.declarative: lexical tones are kept; gradual declination across the phrase, lowering of high targets after a low tone, and extra lowering of the final syllable
intonation.yes_no_question: with the particle ma (neutral tone) or without it, the pitch register of the whole sentence is raised and declination is reduced, with the largest rise on the last syllables; the final tone keeps its shape but is higher and ends higher (Shen 1990; Liu & Xu 2005)
intonation.wh_question: the wh-word is focused: its tones have an expanded pitch range, and the range after it is compressed and lowered
intonation.continuation: non-final phrases end without final lowering, followed by pitch reset at the start of the next phrase; final syllable lengthened
intonation.accent_shape: no pitch accents; focus expands the pitch range of the tones on the focused word (high targets higher, low targets lower) and compresses the range of everything after it (Xu 1999)
intonation.notes: Intonation is carried by register and range changes laid over the tones, not by replacing them.

inventory.name: tone 1, yīnpíng (阴平), high level
inventory.description: High level. After a lower tone it starts below its target and reaches the high level during the first half of the syllable.
inventory.connected_speech: 55; onset pulled toward the end of the preceding tone; slightly lower late in a phrase through declination

inventory.name: tone 2, yángpíng (阳平), high rising
inventory.description: Mid to high rise. The first third of the syllable is level or falls slightly; the rise is concentrated in the later part and the peak is reached at or just after the end of the syllable.
inventory.connected_speech: 35, often 24 to 34 in running speech; between a tone 1 or tone 2 and another full tone it may flatten toward high level at fast rates (Chao 1968)
inventory.duration: long, second longest in citation form

inventory.name: tone 3, shǎngshēng (上声), low (dipping)
inventory.description: Low falling then rising in isolation and before a pause. The essential target is low; the final rise belongs to the pre-pausal form.
inventory.connected_speech: 21 (half third) before tones 1, 2, 4 and before most neutral-tone syllables; 35 before another tone 3; 214 only before a pause, in isolation or under emphasis
inventory.phonation: modal, very often creaky at the low point
inventory.duration: longest in citation form (214); short as the half third (21)

inventory.name: tone 4, qùshēng (去声), high falling
inventory.description: Fall from the top to the bottom of the range; the peak comes shortly after the start of the syllable, not at its very onset.
inventory.connected_speech: 53 (half fourth) before another tone 4; in non-final position the fall often stops short of the floor (52 or 53)
inventory.phonation: modal, may end in creak at the bottom of the range

inventory.name: neutral tone, qīngshēng (轻声)
inventory.description: Toneless weak syllable with no citation form. Its pitch is set by the preceding tone: half-low after tone 1, mid after tone 2, half-high after tone 3, low after tone 4 (Chao 1968). Instrumental studies show short falling contours after tones 1, 2 and 4 and a mid level or slightly rising contour after tone 3.
inventory.connected_speech: a weak mid target approached slowly, so that in a run of neutral-tone syllables pitch drifts from the end of the last full tone toward mid-low over several syllables (Chen & Xu 2006)
inventory.phonation: modal, often lax with low intensity
inventory.duration: short, about half to 60 percent of a full syllable

sandhi: third-tone sandhi: tone 3 becomes a rising tone (35) before another tone 3 (nǐ hǎo is said ní hǎo); listeners cannot reliably tell the result from a lexical tone 2 (Wang & Li 1967)
half third: tone 3 is low falling 21 without the final rise before tones 1, 2, 4 and before most neutral-tone syllables; the full 214 appears only before a pause, in isolation or under emphasis

in runs of three or more third tones the rule follows prosodic grouping: left-branching [[A B] C] gives 35 35 214 (zhǎnlǎnguǎn), right-branching [A [B C]] gives 21 35 214 (xiǎo lǎohǔ), with 35 35 214 also possible at fast rates; long runs are split into two- and three-syllable domains (Shih 1997; Chen 2000; Duanmu 2007)
before a neutral-tone syllable that is underlyingly tone 3, sandhi applies in reduplicated verbs (xiǎngxiang is 35 plus neutral) but not in kinship terms (jiějie is 21 plus neutral)

一 yī: tone 1 (55) in isolation, in counting, in ordinals and at the end of a word; tone 4 (yì, 51) before tones 1, 2 and 3; tone 2 (yí, 35) before tone 4 and before neutral-tone ge (underlyingly tone 4); neutral between reduplicated verbs (kàn yi kàn)
不 bù: tone 4 (51), but tone 2 (bú, 35) before another tone 4; neutral in A-not-A forms and potential complements (hǎo bu hǎo, kàn bu jiàn)
七 qī and 八 bā could become tone 2 before tone 4 in older Beijing speech; now obsolescent
tone 4 before tone 4 is a half fall 53; the second keeps 51 (Chao 1968)
neutral tone: pitch depends on the preceding tone, 2 after tone 1, 3 after tone 2, 4 after tone 3, 1 after tone 4
tone.neutral_tone: Short, weak, toneless syllable (particles such as de, le, ma, ne, suffixes such as zi and men, and the second syllable of many words). Pitch after tone 1 about 2 (a short fall in instrumental work), after tone 2 about 3 (a short fall), after tone 3 about 4 (mid level or slightly rising, continuing the rise that the half third lacks), after tone 4 about 1 (a short low fall). Duration about half to 60 percent of a full syllable, lower intensity, centralised vowel, weakened coda.
tone.notes: Xu (1997), eight male Beijing speakers, ma-ma sequences in carrier sentences: carry-over effects are assimilatory and large, so the onset of each tone is pulled toward the offset of the tone before it and the effect lasts through much of the syllable; anticipatory effects are small and mostly dissimilatory, so a following low onset (tone 3 or tone 2) raises the F0 maximum of the preceding tone. Tone 2 begins level or falling and rises late; tone 4 peaks after syllable onset. Where a tone must start far from where the previous one ended, the contour is distorted and its target is reached late. In his plots the citation tones of the male speakers together span most of an octave. Xu (1999): focus widens the range of the focused word and compresses what follows. The order of citation durations, tone 3 longest, then tone 2, tone 1 and tone 4 shortest, is widely reported (for example Howie 1976).

phonation: creaky voice is frequent at the low point of tone 3 and at the end of tone 4 and helps listeners identify tone 3 (Kuang 2017)
no phonation contrast in consonants; stops and affricates contrast in aspiration only

problems: no sentence intonation: tone languages are routed to CalcPitches_Tone() in src/libespeak-ng/intonation.c, which ignores the clause type; a statement and the same text ending in a question mark give byte-identical audio, and the declination variables are never set, so there is no declination, final lowering or focus

the tonal pitch range is very small: the tone table uses pitch values 9 to 55, which with the voice setting 'pitch 80 118' is about 75 to 99 Hz (under 5 semitones, measured on the output) where natural citation tones span most of an octave

third-tone sandhi is applied to every adjacent pair regardless of prosodic grouping, so a run of third tones is 35 35 ... 214 (小老虎 is 35 35 214 instead of 21 35 214; 我也很想买五把好雨伞 has nine rising tones in a row)

the tone changes of 一 and 不 are not rules: they come from word-pair entries in the optional dictionary dictsource/extra/cmn_listx (about 1,800 entries beginning with 一 and 11,900 with 不); a pair that is not listed keeps the citation tone (一坨 and 一沓 come out with yi1), and without that file every 一 is yi1 and every 不 is bu4
erhua is not implemented and is broken for listed words: entries such as (花 儿) hua1r5 contain a syllable r5 that the rules cannot read, so 花儿, 这儿, 哪儿 and 一点儿 are spelled out in English
no tonal coarticulation: every syllable gets a fixed contour, and the voice attribute 'words 1' puts a short pause between words, so speech is staccato

inside a clause all full tones have the same length whatever the tone, so the half third is not shorter and tone 4 not shorter; only on the last syllable of a clause are tones 2 and 3 longer than tones 1 and 4 (about 290 against 235 ms measured)

the neutral tone is shorter (150 against 230) and lower but keeps full vowel quality; many common neutral-tone words are said with full tones (东西, 朋友), and before a neutral tone from an underlying tone 3 the first syllable is always 21 (想想, 哪里)
x is played with the uvular fricative sample (phoneme X, shown as χ) and r with a voiced retroflex fricative (z.); both are within the attested range but at its edge
the syllables jiong, qiong and xiong are not covered by cmn_rules (the final iong is missing from letter group L03), so characters with these readings (熊, 穷, 兄, 窘) are spelled out in English
good: third-tone sandhi is implemented in C, in CalcPitches_Tone() in src/libespeak-ng/intonation.c: a 214 before another 214 becomes 35, a 214 before any other tone becomes 21, and 214 is kept before a pause; it applies across word boundaries inside a clause
tone 4 before tone 4 inside a word becomes 53
neutral-tone height follows Chao's values exactly: 22 after tone 1, 33 after tone 2, 44 after tone 3, 11 after tone 4
aspirated and unaspirated stops and affricates use separate recorded bursts; the dental, retroflex and alveolo-palatal series are all present
both apical vowels exist (i[ after ts tsh s, i. after the retroflexes)
tone 2 has a late rise and tone 3 a dip placed at about one third of the syllable, as in the literature

notes: The voice sit/cmn has the same settings as sit/cmn-Latn-pinyin: both read Han characters and both read Latin letters as Pinyin with tone digits. The name 'latin as English' of sit/cmn does not match its behaviour, because the voice file has no dictrules line and cmn_rules has no conditional rules.
